title: There Are No Followers in a Complex System
author: Nick Hart
summary: Drawing on Uhl-Bien and colleagues' work on followership, Hart asks what remains of the follower once leadership is understood as an emergent property of complex systems. He restates his position that leadership is the social process of influence rather than a status held by individuals, then turns the usual question around: what do people without formal position do that makes leadership possible at all? Noticing influence that runs upward, sideways and diagonally through the hierarchy of job titles reframes staffroom conversations, curriculum talk and corridor exchanges as constituent parts of the leadership system. From there Hart declares the follower a relic of the industrial age, arguing the role becomes redundant when every interaction either enables or inhibits the emergence of leadership. He is careful not to abolish hierarchy, conceding that someone must set direction, hold accountability and decide. What he rejects is the low-agency framing that the language of following imposes. The final section specifies the conditions on which emergence depends, trust, psychological safety, clarity of purpose and a rhythm of collaboration, and describes what happens when they weaken: meetings become updates, decisions slow, and people wait to be led.
points: Hart inverts followership theory's usual framing, asking not how followers respond to leaders but what those without formal roles contribute that makes leadership emerge in the first place.
The claim that a headteacher cannot make teaching great across a whole school but a connected staff culture can is the argument's practical payoff for anyone weighing policy against relationships.
Weak conditions produce a recognisable pathology described precisely: meetings degrade into updates, decisions slow down, and initiative retreats into formality.
Hart wants followership rebranded rather than defended, on the grounds that the vocabulary of following itself sets a tone of low agency.
Shifting the unit of analysis from individual capacity to interactional quality changes what a school should value and invest in, namely how teams think together and adapt as conditions change.
quotes: Followership theory invites us to look at leadership in the times when people choose to engage, contribute and influence from positions that aren’t formally in charge. It suggests that leadership doesn’t reside in individuals at all, but in relationships.

For schools, this means that every teacher meeting, every curriculum conversation, every informal moment in the corridor is part of the leadership system, all capable of strengthening (or weakening) the emergence of leadership.

Just like the heroic leader, the follower is a relic from the industrial age, following orders and procedures in mechanistic environments. The more we look closely at leadership in complex organisations, especially schools, the role of the follower becomes redundant.
Followership is participation and co-construction and it needs a rebrand. The language of following sets the tone of low agency.

Leadership emerges where people feel able to notice, speak and act on what matters. That emergence depends on conditions of trust, psychological safety, clarity of purpose and a rhythm of collaboration that encourages initiative.
A headteacher can’t make teaching great across a whole school but a connected staff culture can. A policy can’t drive improvement but a shared sense of purpose can.
In a complex system there are no followers, only people in constant conversation about what matters.
